title: Tomato Soup
description: A smooth tomato and basil soup built from canned whole tomatoes, gently softened vegetables, and vegetable broth for a comforting lunch or light supper.
ingredients: 2 cans (28 oz each) whole peeled tomatoes
instructions: Warm the olive oil in a soup pot over medium heat, then add the onion, carrots, and celery with a small pinch of salt.
Cook, stirring now and then, until the vegetables are softened and the onion looks translucent, about 8 minutes.
Add the garlic and tomato paste. Stir for about a minute so the paste cooks onto the vegetables without letting the garlic colour too darkly.
Pour in the tomatoes and all their juices, breaking the tomatoes apart with a spoon as they go into the pot.
Add the vegetable broth, oregano, salt, and pepper, and bring the pot to a calm simmer while scraping any flavourful bits from the base.
Partly cover and cook gently for roughly 25 minutes, until the carrots are very tender and the tomato flavour no longer tastes raw.
Take the pot off the heat, add the basil, and purée with an immersion blender, keeping the blade below the surface throughout.
Taste the soup after blending; use the optional sugar only if the tomatoes taste overly sharp, then adjust salt and pepper.
Warm briefly if needed and serve with toast, crackers, or a grilled cheese sandwich.
tips: Whole canned tomatoes give the soup a dependable base when fresh tomatoes are out of season.
If using a countertop blender, let the soup cool slightly and blend small batches with the lid vented safely.
Season after puréeing, because blending distributes the salt and herbs more evenly.
commonMistakes: Letting garlic scorch can add an unpleasant bitter note to an otherwise mild soup.
A hard boil can cook off too much liquid before the vegetables are fully soft.
Sealing hot soup in a full blender can build pressure and cause splashes.
substitutions: Chicken broth may be used in place of vegetable broth when a vegetarian soup is not required.
Use 1 teaspoon dried basil if fresh basil is unavailable, adding it with the oregano.
Fire-roasted canned tomatoes give the finished soup a subtle charred flavour.
storage: Cool the soup promptly and refrigerate it in a covered container for up to 4 days.
Reheat over low to medium heat, stirring occasionally until hot throughout.
Freeze in individual portions for up to 3 months and defrost in the refrigerator overnight.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura

title: Creamy Tomato Soup
description: Velvety tomato soup enriched with a little cream and Parmesan, balanced by garlic and basil for a fuller, mellow finish.
instructions: Heat the olive oil in a Dutch oven or heavy saucepan over medium heat and add the chopped onion.
Cook until the onion is soft and sweet-smelling, about 6 to 8 minutes, stirring before it begins to brown at the edges.
Stir in the garlic, then dust the vegetables with flour and keep stirring for a minute to cook the flour without darkening it.
Whisk in the vegetable broth gradually until the base is smooth, then stir in crushed tomatoes, sugar, salt, and pepper.
Bring the mixture to a gentle simmer and cook uncovered for around 20 minutes, stirring from the bottom occasionally.
Add the basil, take the pot off the burner, and blend until the soup has no visible vegetable pieces.
Set the heat to low and pour in the cream slowly, stirring continuously; do not allow the soup to bubble hard after this point.
Add Parmesan in small amounts, stirring until smooth after each addition, then taste and adjust the seasoning only if needed.
Ladle into bowls while hot and finish with basil or extra Parmesan if desired.
tips: Removing the pot from the heat briefly makes immersion blending easier to control.
Warm the cream slightly or add it gradually so the soup stays evenly smooth.
Use finely grated Parmesan so it incorporates before the soup cools.
commonMistakes: Boiling dairy-rich soup vigorously can cause a grainy or split appearance.
Skipping the short flour-cooking stage leaves a raw, chalky flavour.
Adding sugar before tasting may make the soup unnecessarily sweet.
substitutions: Half-and-half gives a lighter result than heavy cream.
Chicken broth can replace vegetable broth when a vegetarian version is not needed.
Pecorino Romano is a sharper alternative to Parmesan; use it carefully because it is saltier.
storage: Store cooled soup covered in the refrigerator for up to 4 days.
Rewarm slowly over low to medium-low heat, stirring often and avoiding a boil.
For the most stable frozen result, freeze the tomato base before the cream and Parmesan are stirred in.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura

title: Potato Soup
description: A chunky, creamy potato soup with crisp bacon, cheddar, sour cream, and chives, thickened by mashing part of the cooked potatoes in the pot.
ingredients: 2 1/2 lb russet potatoes, peeled and cubed
instructions: Put the bacon in a cold Dutch oven, then bring it up to medium heat so the pieces render gradually and become crisp.
Lift the bacon onto a paper-lined plate, reserving about 2 tablespoons of fat in the pot.
Add the diced onion to the rendered fat and cook until soft, then stir in the garlic just until fragrant.
Stir flour through the onion mixture for about a minute, coating it evenly so it can thicken the broth without tasting raw.
Whisk in chicken broth a little at a time until smooth, then add potatoes, salt, and pepper.
Simmer with the lid slightly ajar until the potatoes yield easily to a fork, about 15 to 18 minutes, stirring the base from time to time.
Use a potato masher to crush roughly one-third of the cubes in the pot, leaving the rest intact for texture.
Turn the heat to low and stir in milk and sour cream. Add the cheddar in portions until melted, keeping the soup below a boil.
Taste for salt and pepper, then serve with the crisp bacon and chives scattered over each bowl.
tips: Keeping the potato cubes close in size prevents some pieces from collapsing before others are cooked.
A partial mash gives body to the broth without losing the satisfying potato pieces.
Cheese grated from a block tends to melt more smoothly than pre-shredded cheese.
commonMistakes: Puréeing russet potatoes too thoroughly can make their starch turn pasty.
Letting the soup boil after milk, sour cream, or cheese is added can affect its texture.
Adding cheese all at once can make it clump instead of melting evenly.
substitutions: For a meat-free option, use vegetable broth and omit bacon, adding a little olive oil to cook the onion.
Yukon Gold potatoes make a naturally creamier alternative to russets.
Plain Greek yogurt can replace sour cream when stirred in off the heat.
storage: Refrigerate cooled soup in a covered container for up to 4 days.
Warm it gently with a splash of milk or broth to loosen the texture.
Freezing is best avoided because cooked potato and dairy can change texture after thawing.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura

title: Broccoli Cheddar Soup
description: A rich broccoli and cheddar soup with small tender florets, grated carrot, and a smooth cheese base that stays spoonable rather than overly thick.
instructions: Melt butter in a heavy soup pot over medium heat and cook the finely diced onion until soft, taking care not to brown the butter.
Whisk the flour into the onion and cook the paste for 1 to 2 minutes until it smells lightly toasted rather than raw.
Gradually whisk in the vegetable broth, followed by the milk and half-and-half, until the liquid is completely smooth.
Add broccoli, carrot, garlic powder, salt, and pepper, then bring the soup only to a quiet simmer.
Partly cover and cook over medium-low heat until the broccoli stems are tender but the florets have not disappeared, about 15 minutes.
Press a small portion of the cooked broccoli against the side of the pot if a thicker soup is wanted, leaving plenty of pieces whole.
Lower the heat as far as possible and stir in the cheddar a handful at a time, waiting for each addition to melt before adding more.
Check the seasoning and serve while hot, without bringing the cheese soup back to a boil.
tips: Shred a block of cheddar shortly before cooking for the smoothest melt.
Cut large florets in half so the broccoli fits comfortably on a spoon.
Keep the pot at low heat once the cheese goes in to protect the creamy texture.
commonMistakes: High heat after adding cheddar can cause the fat and proteins to separate.
Pouring the broth in too quickly makes it harder to whisk out flour lumps.
Leaving broccoli stems in large chunks may leave them firm when the florets are ready.
substitutions: Chicken broth can be used when a vegetarian soup is not needed.
Mild cheddar gives a softer cheese flavour than sharp cheddar.
Use more whole milk in place of half-and-half for a less rich bowl.
storage: Keep leftovers covered in the refrigerator for up to 3 days.
Reheat slowly on the stovetop, stirring regularly and stopping before it boils.
Freezing is not ideal because the dairy and cheese base may separate after thawing.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura

title: Clam Chowder
description: A New England-inspired clam chowder with tender potato, bacon, thyme, and clams folded into a creamy, savoury broth at the end of cooking.
ingredients: 3 cans (6.5 oz each) chopped clams, drained with liquid reserved
Chopped parsley and oyster crackers, for serving
instructions: Cook the diced bacon in a heavy pot over medium heat until it is crisp, then transfer it to a plate and leave about 2 tablespoons of fat in the pot.
Cook the onion and celery in the bacon fat until softened, then add garlic and stir just until its aroma blooms.
Mix in the flour and keep stirring for a minute so it coats the vegetables and loses its raw taste.
Whisk in clam juice, the reserved clam liquid, and chicken broth gradually until the base is smooth.
Add the potatoes, thyme, and bay leaf. Simmer partly covered until the potatoes are tender but still hold their cubes, about 15 to 18 minutes.
Turn the heat low and stir in the cream, warming gently without letting the chowder boil.
Add drained clams and most of the bacon, then heat only until the clams are warmed through, about 2 to 3 minutes.
Discard the bay leaf, taste before adding salt, and serve with parsley, remaining bacon, and oyster crackers.
tips: The liquid from canned clams adds flavour, so measure it into the pot along with the clam juice.
Wait until the potatoes are tender before adding clams, which need only brief warming.
Cut the potatoes to similar size so they finish at the same time.
commonMistakes: Simmering clams for too long makes them firm and chewy.
Boiling a cream-based chowder after the dairy is added can affect its texture.
Seasoning aggressively before tasting can make the chowder too salty because clam liquid varies.
substitutions: Russet potatoes give a softer texture and release more starch into the broth.
Additional clam juice may replace the chicken broth for a stronger seafood note.
Half-and-half can replace heavy cream for a lighter chowder.
storage: Refrigerate leftovers promptly in a covered container for up to 3 days.
Reheat over low heat until steaming, without bringing the chowder to a boil.
Freezing is not recommended because potato and cream textures can deteriorate after thawing.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura

title: Chicken Tortilla Soup
description: A vibrant chicken tortilla soup with black beans, corn, fire-roasted tomatoes, warm spices, and crunchy tortilla strips added at the table.
ingredients: Avocado, cilantro, and lime wedges, for serving
instructions: Heat 1 tablespoon of oil in a soup pot over medium heat and cook the onion and jalapeño until tender, about 6 minutes.
Add garlic, cumin, and chili powder, stirring for about 30 seconds so the spices become fragrant without burning.
Pour in the fire-roasted tomatoes and chicken broth, loosening any flavourful bits on the bottom of the pot as the liquid warms.
Stir in black beans and corn, then simmer partly covered for 15 minutes to bring the broth together.
Add the cooked shredded chicken and warm it through for about 5 minutes rather than cooking it for a long time.
In a separate wide skillet, heat the remaining oil and fry the tortilla strips in batches until crisp and golden. Drain and lightly salt them.
Stir lime juice into the soup, then taste and make small adjustments to salt, cumin, or lime as needed.
Serve the soup with avocado, cilantro, lime wedges, and tortilla strips added at the last moment.
tips: Shredded rotisserie chicken makes this soup especially quick to assemble.
Keep the tortilla strips separate until serving so they remain crisp.
Removing jalapeño seeds and membranes reduces the heat while keeping its fresh pepper flavour.
commonMistakes: Leaving already-cooked chicken at a hard simmer for too long can dry it out.
Adding tortilla strips early lets them absorb broth and lose their crunch.
Skipping the rinse on canned beans can cloud the broth.
substitutions: Pinto beans are a suitable alternative to black beans.
Use cooked turkey in place of chicken when available.
For baked strips, toss tortillas lightly with oil and bake at 400°F until crisp, watching closely.
storage: Refrigerate the cooled soup base without toppings for up to 4 days.
Reheat until hot throughout, then finish each bowl with fresh toppings.
Freeze the soup base for up to 3 months; make tortilla strips and add avocado after reheating.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura

title: Taco Soup
description: A hearty one-pot taco soup with browned beef, two kinds of beans, corn, tomatoes, and build-your-own Tex-Mex toppings.
ingredients: 1 can (10 oz) tomatoes with green chiles
Shredded cheese, sour cream, avocado, and tortilla chips, for serving
instructions: Warm the oil in a large soup pot over medium-high heat, then cook the ground beef and onion together, breaking the beef into small pieces as it browns.
If there is a large amount of rendered fat, drain it carefully. Stir in garlic and taco seasoning until the mixture smells fragrant.
Add diced tomatoes, tomatoes with green chiles, and beef broth, scraping the bottom of the pot to lift the browned flavour into the soup.
Mix in black beans, pinto beans, corn, and salt, then bring the pot to a light boil.
Lower to a steady simmer and cook uncovered for about 20 minutes, stirring occasionally as the broth becomes slightly more substantial.
Confirm the beef is cooked and the beans are hot, then taste before adding any more salt because seasoning levels vary between canned ingredients.
Let the pot stand off the heat for 5 minutes to settle before serving.
Serve with cheese, sour cream, avocado, and tortilla chips on the side so each bowl can be finished to taste.
tips: Rinsing canned beans helps keep the soup cleaner-tasting and reduces some surface sodium.
Give the beef time to brown before adding broth for a more savoury base.
A topping bar keeps chips crunchy and makes the soup easy to adapt for different diners.
commonMistakes: Too much beef fat left in the pot can make the broth feel greasy.
Adding salt before tasting can oversalt a soup already seasoned by taco mix and canned tomatoes.
Adding avocado, dairy, or chips while the soup cooks removes the contrast those toppings provide.
substitutions: Ground turkey is a leaner swap for ground beef.
Kidney beans can replace pinto beans without changing the method.
Add finely chopped jalapeño with the onion for additional heat.
storage: Cool and refrigerate the plain soup in a covered container for up to 4 days.
Keep avocado, dairy toppings, and tortilla chips separate until serving.
Freeze the soup base without toppings for up to 3 months.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura

title: French Onion Soup
description: A French-inspired onion soup of slowly browned onions and savoury broth, finished with toasted baguette and a golden Gruyère topping.
instructions: Melt the butter and olive oil together in a wide, heavy pot. Add sliced onions and salt, turning until every slice has a light coating of fat.
Cook over medium-low heat for 40 to 50 minutes, stirring increasingly often as the onions shrink and turn deep golden brown.
When the onions are soft and well coloured, add sugar and garlic; stir briefly so neither catches on the base of the pot.
Pour in white wine and scrape the pot thoroughly. Let it reduce for a few minutes until the alcohol scent has mellowed.
Add beef broth, thyme, bay leaf, Worcestershire sauce, and black pepper, then simmer uncovered for 25 minutes.
Meanwhile, toast baguette slices at 400°F until crisp and dry on both sides.
Remove the bay leaf and adjust seasoning. Place broiler-safe bowls on a rimmed baking sheet and fill them with hot soup.
Set two baguette slices over each bowl, blanket them with Gruyère, and broil under close watch until the cheese is bubbling with browned spots.
tips: The onions develop their sweetness slowly, so keep the heat moderate and allow time for the colour to build.
Confirm that bowls are rated safe for broiling before putting them under the element.
Crisp toast holds up better beneath the melted cheese than soft bread.
commonMistakes: High heat can burn onion edges before the centres have a chance to caramelize.
Using a cramped pot holds in steam and slows browning.
The cheese can brown very fast under a broiler, so do not leave it unattended.
substitutions: Swiss cheese can take the place of Gruyère.
Use an equal amount of broth in place of white wine if avoiding wine.
Vegetable broth offers a vegetarian-friendly variation, provided Worcestershire is also replaced with a suitable alternative.
storage: Refrigerate the plain soup separately from bread and cheese for up to 4 days.
Heat the soup first, then make a fresh toast-and-cheese topping when serving leftovers.
Freeze the soup without bread or cheese for up to 3 months.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura

title: Beef Barley Soup
description: A slow-simmered beef and barley soup with browned chuck, tender vegetables, pearl barley, and a deeply savoury broth.
ingredients: 2 lb beef chuck, cut into 1-inch cubes
instructions: Blot the beef cubes dry, season with salt and pepper, and heat 1 tablespoon olive oil in a Dutch oven over medium-high heat.
Sear the beef in two roomy batches until several sides are deeply browned, then transfer each batch to a plate.
Reduce the heat to medium and cook the onion, carrots, and celery in the remaining oil, scraping the browned residue from the pot as the vegetables soften.
Stir in garlic and tomato paste for about a minute, allowing the paste to darken slightly without scorching the garlic.
Return the beef and any juices to the pot. Add broth, thyme, bay leaves, and Worcestershire sauce, then bring to a calm simmer.
Simmer partly covered for 45 minutes. Add rinsed pearl barley and continue cooking for 40 to 45 minutes, until both the beef and barley are tender.
Stir the soup a few times toward the end, adding a little water or broth if the barley has made the soup thicker than you prefer.
Remove the bay leaves, correct the seasoning, and finish with parsley before serving.
tips: A dry beef surface and an uncrowded pot make browning easier and enrich the broth.
Rinse pearl barley in a fine sieve before it goes into the pot.
Expect barley to continue absorbing liquid after refrigeration, so keep extra broth on hand for leftovers.
commonMistakes: Putting all the beef in at once cools the pot and causes steaming instead of browning.
Adding pearl barley at the beginning can leave it too soft by the time the beef is tender.
Neglecting to stir late in cooking can allow barley to settle at the bottom.
substitutions: Prepared stew meat is a practical alternative when chuck is unavailable.
Quick-cooking barley can be used, but add it according to its package timing.
Sliced mushrooms can join the vegetables for an extra savoury element.
storage: Refrigerate cooled soup in a covered container for up to 4 days.
Reheat with a splash of broth or water because the barley continues to thicken the soup.
Freeze in airtight single portions for up to 3 months.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura

title: Split Pea Soup
description: Classic split pea soup simmered with smoky ham, tender vegetables, and herbs until naturally thick and comforting.
ingredients: 1 lb dried green split peas, sorted and rinsed
1 meaty ham bone or smoked ham hock
instructions: Spread the split peas on a tray, remove any small stones or damaged peas, and rinse them under cool water until the draining water runs mostly clear.
Heat the oil in a large heavy pot over medium heat, add the onion, carrots, and celery, and cook for 7 minutes until softened but not deeply browned.
Stir in the garlic and thyme for 30 seconds, then add the split peas, ham bone, chicken broth, bay leaf, and black pepper.
Bring the pot to a gentle boil, skim away any foam from the surface, then reduce the heat so the soup maintains a quiet, steady simmer.
Partially cover and cook for 60 to 75 minutes, stirring more frequently as the peas soften, until they break down and the soup becomes thick and creamy.
Transfer the ham bone to a plate, remove usable meat when cool enough to handle, and discard the bone, skin, and any large pieces of fat.
Return the picked meat and diced cooked ham to the pot, simmer for another 5 minutes, and add broth or water if the texture is thicker than preferred.
Remove the bay leaf, taste before adding salt because ham can be salty, then serve hot with black pepper and crusty bread.
tips: Split peas do not need soaking, but they must be sorted and rinsed.
Stir often once the soup begins to thicken.
Season with salt only after the ham has flavored the broth.
commonMistakes: High heat can scorch thick pea soup on the bottom.
Salting early may make a ham-based soup too salty.
Old dried peas may require extra simmering time.
substitutions: Use a smoked turkey leg instead of ham.
Use vegetable broth and omit meat for a vegetarian soup.
Add a diced potato for an even heartier texture.
storage: Refrigerate cooled soup for up to 4 days.
Thin with broth or water while reheating.
Freeze in airtight portions for up to 3 months.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura
